period: 30th Dynasty, Nectanebo I, c. 370 BC; kiosk of Taharqa, 25th Dynasty, 690-664 BC
summary: Karnak's front gate is its newest and was never finished: the builders' mud-brick ramp still leans against it after more than 2,000 years.
look: The first pylon is 113 metres wide and 15 metres thick, its surface left rough and uncarved. Inside, the Great Court opens up: on the left the small triple shrine of Seti II, on the right the temple of Ramesses III, and in the middle the single tall column of Taharqa's kiosk. Turn round once inside to see the mud-brick ramp against the back of the south tower, on your left as you face the gate.
story:
The gate you have just walked through is the last great addition to Karnak's main axis, begun under Nectanebo I of the 30th Dynasty and never completed. Its faces were never smoothed or carved, and against the back of the south tower lies the best evidence we have of how pylons were built: a slope of mud brick, the remains of the builders' ramp. Blocks were dragged up it course by course, and the ramp would have been cleared away at the end. Here the end never came.

Behind lies the Great Court, the largest at Karnak. Before it existed, this space was an open approach lined with ram sphinxes; when the court was walled in, they were moved to the sides, where they still lie in rows.

In the middle stands one great column with an open papyrus capital, about 21 metres high. It is the last of ten that formed the kiosk of Taharqa, a king from Kush, in modern Sudan, who ruled Egypt from 690 to 664 BC, when Kushite kings ruled the whole Nile valley. The kiosk was a stopping place for Amun's boat on its way through the court. Later kings, Psamtik II and Ptolemy IV, added their names to the column.

On your left is the small triple shrine of Seti II, three chapels where the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu could rest. On your right, the temple of Ramesses III juts out of the court's south wall.
details: Inside, turn round: against the back of the south tower, on your left, are the remains of the mud-brick building ramp.
In the middle of the court, Taharqa's single column: compare its open papyrus capital with the Hypostyle's central columns.
Rows of ram sphinxes line the north and south sides of the court, moved there when the court was built.
In the gate passage, look for the inscription carved by the scholars of Napoleon's expedition, listing positions of Egypt's temples.
Left: Seti II's triple shrine. Right: the temple of Ramesses III, with the Bubastite Portal just beyond it.
fun_fact: Taharqa appears in the Bible as Tirhakah, king of Cush, who marched out against the Assyrian king Sennacherib.
narration:
You have just walked through the first pylon, the giant gate of Karnak. It is 113 metres wide, and it is the newest building on this axis, begun around 370 BC under Nectanebo the First. It was never finished.

Turn round and look at the back of the tower on your left. That sloping heap of mud brick is what remains of the builders' ramp. The Egyptians built pylons by dragging blocks up ramps like this, layer by layer, and then removed the ramp. Here they stopped, and so left us the best evidence of how it was done.

Now turn back to the court. It is the largest at Karnak. The rams along its sides once lined an open avenue, and were pushed aside when the court was built.

In the middle stands one enormous column, about 21 metres high, with a capital like an open papyrus flower. It is the last of ten columns of a kiosk built by Taharqa, a king from Kush in modern Sudan, who ruled Egypt from 690 to 664 BC. The Bible knows him as Tirhakah. The kiosk was a resting place for Amun's sacred boat.

On your left is a small triple shrine of Seti the Second, with chapels for the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu. On your right, a complete little temple of Ramesses the Third sticks out of the court wall.

Walk to the base of Taharqa's column and look up. It gives you the scale of the hall waiting beyond the next gate.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, Ramesses III, c. 1186-1155 BC; Bubastite Portal c. 925 BC
summary: A complete temple in miniature, built as a resting place for Amun's boat; next door, a pharaoh's victory list that names towns from the Bible.
look: On the right-hand, south side of the Great Court, the temple's small pylon opens into a court lined with pillars, each fronted by a standing statue of the king as Osiris. Beyond are a small columned hall and three chapels for the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu. Just east of it, against the second pylon, is the Bubastite Portal; Sheshonq I's relief and list of towns are on the outer wall beside it.
story:
Ramesses III, the last great warrior king of the New Kingdom, built this as a barque station: a place where the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu could stop on their way in and out of the temple. It is a full temple shrunk to fit: a pylon with the king smiting his enemies, an open court with Osiride pillars, a hall, and three small sanctuaries. If you visited his huge temple at Medinet Habu on the West Bank, you will recognise the style. When it was built it stood free in front of Karnak; later the Great Court was walled around it.

Next door is the Bubastite Portal, named after the 22nd Dynasty kings from Bubastis in the Delta. Their founder, Sheshonq I, of Libyan descent, campaigned in Palestine around 925 BC, and on the wall outside he is shown smiting captives before Amun above rows of name rings, one for each town he claimed. Most scholars identify him with Shishak, the pharaoh who, according to the Bible, came up against Jerusalem in the fifth year of King Rehoboam. One ring has been read as 'the heights of David', a reading that is still disputed.
details: On the small pylon, look for Ramesses III smiting a bunch of enemies before Amun.
In the court, the Osiride pillars: the king as Osiris, arms crossed on his chest.
At the back, three small chapels side by side, for Amun, Mut and Khonsu.
Outside the Bubastite Portal: rows of oval name rings, each topped by a bound captive and filled with a town's name.
fun_fact: Jerusalem, the city the Bible says Shishak marched against, does not seem to appear on his list: one of the long-running puzzles of biblical archaeology.
narration:
On the right side of the great court is a whole temple in miniature, built by Ramesses the Third around 1180 BC. If you visited his huge temple at Medinet Habu on the West Bank, you will recognise the style.

It was a resting station for the sacred boats. At the gate the king smites his enemies. Inside is an open court lined with statues of Ramesses as Osiris, then a small hall, then three chapels side by side for the boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu.

Just beyond it, by the second pylon, is the Bubastite Portal. On the wall outside, Sheshonq the First, a king of Libyan descent, celebrated his campaign in Palestine around 925 BC. He smites his captives before Amun, and below are rows of oval rings, each topped by a bound prisoner and filled with the name of a captured town. Most scholars think Sheshonq is the pharaoh Shishak of the Bible, who marched against Jerusalem.

Strangely, Jerusalem does not seem to be on his list. Look at the rows of name rings, and count how many towns one campaign could claim.

period: New Kingdom, Horemheb to Ramesses II, c. 1300-1250 BC; colossus reinscribed c. 1050 BC
summary: A gate stuffed with the demolished temples of Akhenaten, guarded by a Ramesses II colossus that a priest-king later claimed as his own.
look: The second pylon, much ruined, stands at the east end of the Great Court with a tall gateway leading into the Hypostyle Hall. To the left of the gate stands a pink granite colossus, 10.5 metres high, of a king holding crook and flail, with a small female figure in front of his legs. Colossi of Ramesses II also stand by the doorway.
story:
The second pylon was raised by Horemheb, the general who became king at the end of the 18th Dynasty, and taken over by Ramesses I and Ramesses II. Horemheb had a convenient source of stone: the temples Akhenaten had built at Karnak for the Aten, now being pulled down. Thousands of their small, standard-sized blocks, the talatat, were packed inside this pylon as fill. By hiding them, he preserved them. Archaeologists have been taking them out and studying them ever since, and one reassembled wall stands in the Luxor Museum.

The colossus by the gate was made for Ramesses II. About 200 years later Pinedjem I, High Priest of Amun, put his name on it. By then the pharaohs ruled from the Delta, and in Thebes the high priests of Amun governed in all but name; Pinedjem went further and took the title of king over Upper Egypt. His son Psusennes I became pharaoh at Tanis, and other sons became high priests at Thebes, among them Masaharta, whose mummy you can see in the Mummification Museum.
details: Left of the gate: the pink granite colossus, with a small princess or queen standing in front of the king's legs.
Look at the cartouches on the colossus: the name carved there is Pinedjem's, not Ramesses'.
In the gateway, look for reliefs of Ptolemaic kings, who repaired the passage long after Horemheb.
Step through the gate and stop: the first view of the Hypostyle Hall's columns is one to remember.
fun_fact: Horemheb used Akhenaten's demolished temples as rubble, and that is exactly why so much of the heretic king's art survives: it was hidden inside his enemy's gate.
narration:
This is the second pylon, the gate into the great hall. It was built by Horemheb, the general who became king, and taken over by the first Ramesside kings.

Horemheb had a cheap source of stone. The temples Akhenaten had built here for the sun disc were being demolished, and thousands of their small, standard blocks were packed inside this pylon as fill. By hiding them, he preserved them. Archaeologists have pulled many out, and you can see one rebuilt wall in the Luxor Museum.

To the left of the gate stands a pink granite colossus, 10.5 metres high, with a small woman, a princess or queen, standing in front of the king's legs. It was carved for Ramesses the Second. But about 200 years later another man put his name on it: Pinedjem, High Priest of Amun. By then the pharaohs lived far away in the Delta, and here in Thebes the priests of Amun ruled in all but name. Pinedjem eventually called himself king.

Look at the little woman at the giant's feet, then step through the gate into the forest of columns.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Seti I and Ramesses II, c. 1290-1250 BC
summary: 134 columns on 5,000 square metres: a papyrus swamp in stone, begun by Seti I and finished, partly in his own name, by his son Ramesses II.
look: You are in a hall of 134 columns in 16 rows. The 12 along the central aisle are the giants, over 20 metres tall with open papyrus capitals; the other 122, about 14 metres, end in closed buds. Above the central aisle, stone window grilles of the clerestory survive, and in places paint still clings to the capitals and the undersides of the architraves.
story:
The hall is a picture of creation. Egyptians believed the world began as a mound rising from the waters of Nun, with papyrus growing in the marsh around it; these columns are that marsh in stone.

Earlier scholars credited Amenhotep III or Horemheb, but today the hall is attributed to Seti I, who built it and decorated the northern half around 1290 BC. His son Ramesses II finished the southern half, and you can tell them apart. Seti's carving, on your left as you face east, is fine raised relief. Ramesses began in raised relief too, then switched to sunk relief, quicker to cut and bolder in strong sun, and in places he put his own name over his father's work. Later, Ramesses IV and the High Priest Herihor squeezed their names into the gaps.

The central aisle stood higher than the rest, and grilled clerestory windows let shafts of light into it while the side aisles stayed dim.

Groundwater is the enemy. In 1899 eleven columns collapsed in a chain reaction after their foundations were undermined. Georges Legrain rebuilt them, finishing in May 1902, and the rest of the columns have since been strengthened. The hall stayed in use for some seventeen centuries, until the 4th century AD.
details: North half, left as you face east: Seti I's delicate raised relief. South half: Ramesses II's deeper sunk relief.
Look up between the central columns: the stone window grilles of the clerestory still survive.
In the shade under the architraves and on the capitals, look for surviving traces of ancient paint.
On the walls, find priests carrying the boat of Amun on poles, the same procession you saw at Luxor Temple.
For the classic photo, stand at a corner of the central aisle and shoot diagonally across the rows.
fun_fact: In 1899 eleven columns fell like dominoes after groundwater undermined them; Georges Legrain spent three years putting them back. Guides like to say fifty people could stand on top of one central capital.
narration:
You are standing in the Great Hypostyle Hall. There are 134 columns here, in 16 rows, on about 5,000 square metres. The twelve along the central aisle are the giants, more than 20 metres tall, with capitals shaped like open papyrus flowers. Guides like to say fifty people could stand on top of one. The other 122 are shorter, with closed buds.

The idea is a papyrus marsh in stone. Egyptians believed the world began as a mound rising from the waters, with papyrus growing all around it. Every temple recreated that first morning of creation.

The hall was built by Seti the First around 1290 BC and finished by his son, Ramesses the Second, and you can tell their work apart. On the north side, to your left as you face east, Seti's carving is delicate raised relief. On the south side, Ramesses switched to sunk relief, cut into the wall, faster to make and bold in the sun. In places he even put his own name over his father's work.

Once there was a roof. The central aisle stood higher, and stone window grilles let in thin shafts of light, while the side aisles stayed in deep shade.

In 1899 eleven columns fell like dominoes, their foundations rotted by groundwater. Georges Legrain spent three years putting them back.

Now look up between the central columns, at the top of the wall: you can still see some of those stone window grilles.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Seti I and Ramesses II, c. 1290-1258 BC
summary: The outer walls of the great hall are war reporting: Seti I's campaigns on the north side, Ramesses II's Kadesh on the south, and the text of a peace treaty.
look: Leave the hall by its north door and look back at the outer north wall: Seti I's battle scenes, best in low, raking light. Ramesses II's Kadesh scenes run along the outer south wall, and the Egyptian text of his treaty with the Hittites is carved on a wall adjoining it.
story:
Seti I spent much of his first decade fighting in western Asia and Libya, and these north wall reliefs are the main record of it. In his first year he marched out along the Ways of Horus, the military road across northern Sinai, a chain of forts each with its own well, and the carvers drew it almost like a map, fort after fort. On the way he fought the Shasu Bedouin, then took towns in Canaan. Other scenes show him defeating Libyans and fighting a Hittite army. At the end he drives his prisoners home and presents them, with the spoils, to Amun.

On the south side his son told his own story: Kadesh in Syria, May 1274 BC, against the Hittite king Muwatalli II, with some 5,000 to 6,000 chariots on the field. Both sides claimed victory.

About 15 years later, in Ramesses' year 21, 1258 BC, Egypt made peace with the next Hittite king, Hattusili III. The Egyptian version is carved here. A clay tablet of the Hittite version, found at Hattusa, is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum, and a large replica hangs at the United Nations in New York.
details: Outer north wall: Seti I in his chariot as the Shasu scatter; look for the forts of the Ways of Horus drawn in a line.
Find Seti returning to Karnak with rows of bound prisoners, presenting them and the spoils to Amun.
Outer south wall: Ramesses II's version of Kadesh, with chariots and the river Orontes.
On the wall adjoining the south side: long columns of hieroglyphs, the Egyptian text of the Hittite peace treaty.
Come early or late: low sun across these walls shows the shallow carving best.
fun_fact: Each side kept its own copy of the treaty, and, roughly speaking, each copy has the other king asking for peace first.
narration:
The outside walls of the Hypostyle Hall are a war report. On the north side, the wall behind you as you step out of the north door, Seti the First recorded his campaigns from around 1290 BC. He marches out along the Ways of Horus, the military road across Sinai, and the sculptors drew it almost like a map, fort after fort, each with its well. Then come the battles: against the Shasu nomads, the towns of Canaan, the Libyans, and a Hittite army. At the end, the king drags his prisoners home and presents them to Amun.

Around on the south wall, his son Ramesses the Second told the story of Kadesh, the great chariot battle against the Hittites in 1274 BC. Both sides claimed victory. About 15 years later the two empires made peace, and the Egyptian text of that treaty is carved on a wall near here. A copy of the Hittite version hangs at the United Nations, as one of the oldest peace treaties known.

Look along this wall in the low light, and find Seti in his chariot, horses rearing, as his enemies scatter.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Thutmose I c. 1500 BC and Hatshepsut c. 1460 BC
summary: Hatshepsut's obelisk, nearly 30 metres of a single granite block, is the tallest ancient obelisk still standing in Egypt, and her stepson's walls kept it safe.
look: Past the third pylon stands Thutmose I's obelisk, about 21 metres tall, the survivor of a pair. Beyond the fourth pylon rises Hatshepsut's, nearly 30 metres of pink Aswan granite, in the ruined hall between the fourth and fifth pylons. Her long dedication runs round the base in columns of hieroglyphs.
story:
Thutmose I, Hatshepsut's father, set up a pair of obelisks before the gateway of his day around 1500 BC. One still stands, 21.2 metres high and nearly 150 tonnes.

His daughter outdid him. Hatshepsut, who ruled as king from about 1479 to 1458 BC, raised twin obelisks here that were, when built, the tallest in the world. One still stands, nearly 30 metres high and weighing over 300 tonnes; its partner fell and broke, and its top now lies by the Sacred Lake. On the base she speaks in the first person: she was sitting in the palace, thinking of the god who made her, and she wonders what people will say in years to come when they see her monument. The quarrying, she says, took seven months, and the tips were sheathed in electrum, an alloy of gold and silver, to catch the sun.

After her death her stepson Thutmose III had her names and images attacked, but he did not topple her obelisks. He walled them in, hiding much of their height from view, and the masonry protected them.

In 1830 Muhammad Ali offered this obelisk to Britain in place of the Luxor pair. The swap was a French idea, inspired by Champollion, who knew perfectly well it could not be extracted. It is still here.
details: Between the third and fourth pylons: Thutmose I's obelisk, the older and smaller of the two.
At the base of Hatshepsut's obelisk, find the columns of her first-person dedication.
Look for traces of the masonry that Thutmose III built around her obelisk to hide it.
Near the top of the shaft, small scenes show the king offering to Amun.
fun_fact: The tallest ancient obelisk standing anywhere, the Lateran obelisk in Rome, also came from Karnak: the emperor Constantius II shipped it to Rome in AD 357.
narration:
Look up. The tallest obelisk here, nearly 30 metres of a single piece of pink granite from Aswan, belongs to Hatshepsut, the woman who ruled Egypt as king from about 1479 to 1458 BC. It is the tallest ancient obelisk still standing in Egypt.

The smaller one, back near the previous gate, belonged to her father, Thutmose the First. It is about 21 metres high. Hatshepsut made sure hers was bigger.

On the base of her obelisk she speaks in the first person. She tells how she sat in her palace thinking of the god who created her, and how she wonders what people will say in years to come when they see her monument. She says the work in the quarry took seven months. The tips were covered in electrum, a mix of gold and silver, so that they blazed in the sun.

After her death, her stepson Thutmose the Third tried to erase her memory. But he did not pull this down. He built walls around it, hiding it from view, and the walls kept it safe.

Two more stories. In 1830 Egypt's ruler, Muhammad Ali, offered this very obelisk to the British instead of the Luxor pair, knowing it was almost impossible to get out. And the tallest ancient obelisk standing anywhere, now in Rome, was also taken from Karnak.

Now look at the base for the columns of her inscription, and imagine the tip shining like a flame.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Hatshepsut, c. 1460 BC
summary: The top of Hatshepsut's second obelisk rests by the Sacred Lake, so you can see at eye level carving that was meant for the sky.
look: Near the north-west corner of the Sacred Lake, close to the giant scarab, the upper section of Hatshepsut's fallen obelisk is displayed on a low base. You can walk right up to it. On one face the god Amun crowns the kneeling king; at the top is the small pyramid of the tip.
story:
Hatshepsut's obelisks stood as a pair. One still stands in the temple, nearly 30 metres tall; this one fell and broke, and its upper part ended up here by the lake. It is one of the best chances in Egypt to see obelisk carving close up. These reliefs were meant to be read from far below, yet they are as crisp and careful as anything made for eye level.

On one face the god Amun places his hands on the crown of a kneeling king. The king is Hatshepsut, shown as a man, because that was how a pharaoh looked. The scene is the message of her whole reign: Amun himself crowned her.

At the very top is the pyramidion, the small pyramid where the first rays of the sun were believed to strike. In her day it was covered in electrum.
details: Find Amun with his hands on the crown of the kneeling Hatshepsut, shown as a male king.
Look at the pyramidion at the tip, where the electrum cap once caught the first sunlight.
Run your eye along the edges of the hieroglyphs: hard granite, carved this sharply by hand.
Turn round: the giant scarab stands a few steps away.
fun_fact: This granite was cut out at Aswan with balls of harder stone, pounded by hand: the Unfinished Obelisk you saw in Aswan shows the method.
narration:
Here, near the Sacred Lake, is the top of Hatshepsut's second obelisk. Its twin still stands back in the temple, nearly 30 metres tall. This one fell and broke, and so you can do something almost impossible: look an obelisk in the eye.

The carving was meant to be seen from far below, yet it is as careful as anything you will see at eye level. On one face, the god Amun places his hands on the crown of a kneeling king. That king is Hatshepsut. She is shown as a man, with a man's body and kilt, because that is what a pharaoh looked like. The message of the scene is the message of her whole reign: the god himself crowned me.

At the very top is the pyramidion, the little pyramid where the first rays of the sun were believed to land. In her day it was covered in electrum, a mix of gold and silver, and it blazed.

Now find Amun's hands, resting on Hatshepsut's crown.

period: Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty, c. 1950 BC; granite sanctuary of Philip Arrhidaeus, c. 320 BC
summary: Karnak's holy of holies: a granite boat shrine in the name of Alexander's half-brother, and behind it the empty ground of the very first temple.
look: Past the sixth pylon and the two granite pillars of Thutmose III stands the long granite sanctuary of the sacred boat, with painted reliefs still visible inside. Behind it lies a wide, nearly empty court of low foundations: the Middle Kingdom court. The walls around the sanctuary carry Thutmose III's Annals of his campaigns.
story:
The barque sanctuary at the heart of Karnak was rebuilt in granite in the name of Philip III Arrhidaeus, Alexander the Great's half-brother, who reigned from 323 to 317 BC. It replaced an older shrine of Thutmose III, and inside, its reliefs keep much of their colour.

Behind it stood the first Karnak: the temple of Senusret I, built around 1950 BC. Its stone was reused by later kings, and almost nothing is left above the foundations. Since 2002 the French-Egyptian centre at Karnak has traced mud-brick foundations of a complex about 70 metres wide and over 100 metres long.

On the walls around the sanctuary, Thutmose III listed his campaigns in Asia and the tribute they brought: the Annals.
details: Before the sanctuary: two granite pillars of Thutmose III, carved with the lily of the south and the papyrus of the north.
Look inside the granite sanctuary for painted reliefs of Philip as pharaoh, colours still visible.
On the walls around the sanctuary, columns of text: Thutmose III's Annals.
Walk into the empty court behind: this open ground was the first temple of Amun.
fun_fact: Philip Arrhidaeus almost certainly never set foot in Egypt: Egyptian priests built in the name of a Macedonian king they had never seen.
narration:
You are at the heart of Karnak. The long granite building is the sanctuary where Amun's sacred boat rested. The name on it is Philip Arrhidaeus, half-brother of Alexander the Great, who reigned after him from 323 BC. He probably never saw Egypt, but the priests built in his name, and inside the colours are still bright.

Behind it is an almost empty court. This bare ground is the oldest part of Karnak, where Senusret the First built a temple around 1950 BC. Later kings reused its stone, and only foundations remain.

Before you go on, find the two granite pillars in front of the sanctuary: one carved with the lily of the south, the other with the papyrus of the north.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Thutmose III, mid-15th century BC
summary: Thutmose III's jubilee hall has columns carved like the poles of an army tent, and a room of exotic plants and animals he saw in Syria.
look: At the far east end of the main axis, the hall lies across your path: a central nave of columns shaped like tent poles, wider at the top than the bottom, surrounded by lower square pillars. The original entrance is in the south-west corner. On some columns you can see painted Christian saints with haloes; the Botanical Garden room lies behind the main hall.
story:
Thutmose III, Hatshepsut's stepson, ruled alone for over 30 years after her death and led around 17 campaigns into Syria and Palestine. He built this hall at the eastern end of the temple, probably for his jubilee, the Sed festival that renewed a king's strength; it later played a part in the Opet festival, and its exact use is still debated. The Egyptians called it Akh-menu, usually translated 'most glorious of monuments'.

The columns are the surprise. Instead of papyrus or lotus, they copy the wooden poles of a tent, swelling towards the top. The whole hall seems to echo a great tent shrine, awnings and all, as if the soldier king had brought his campaign tent home in stone.

In a small room off the hall, Thutmose was shown offering to 61 royal ancestors. In 1843 the French artist Emile Prisse d'Avennes took the blocks down, by his own account to keep them from the Prussian expedition of Lepsius, and the Karnak King List is now in the Louvre.

Behind the hall is the Botanical Garden: low reliefs of plants, flowers, birds and animals from the king's Syrian campaign of his year 25. Some can be identified; others look garbled in the retelling. Christians later used the hall as a church, and painted saints still look down from the columns.
details: The tent-pole columns: notice how they swell towards the top, like the wooden poles of a tent.
Look for painted Christian saints with haloes on the columns, from the days when this was a church.
Behind the hall, the Botanical Garden: plants, birds and animals carved in low relief along the walls.
Find the small Chamber of Ancestors off the hall: its King List blocks were removed to the Louvre in 1843.
fun_fact: The Botanical Garden has been called the world's first natural-history catalogue: a king who recorded not only the enemies he beat but the flowers he saw.
narration:
You have reached the far eastern end of Karnak, the festival hall of Thutmose the Third. He called it Akh menu, usually translated as the most glorious of monuments.

Thutmose was Hatshepsut's stepson. After her death he ruled alone for more than 30 years and led around 17 campaigns into Syria and Palestine. He built this hall around 1450 BC, probably for his jubilee, the festival that renewed a king's strength, though its exact purpose is still debated.

Look at the columns. They are not papyrus or lotus, like everywhere else. They copy the wooden poles of a tent, thicker at the top than at the bottom. It is as if the soldier king had his campaign tent turned into stone.

Off the hall was a small room where Thutmose made offerings to 61 royal ancestors. In 1843 the Frenchman Emile Prisse d'Avennes took the blocks down and shipped them to Paris, and the Karnak King List is now in the Louvre.

Behind the hall is the room known as the Botanical Garden. Its walls show the plants, flowers, birds and animals the king saw on his campaign in Syria in the 25th year of his reign. Some species can be identified. Others look like a traveller's tall tale.

Much later, Christians turned this hall into a church. Look up at the columns: you can still see painted saints, with haloes, looking down at you.

period: New Kingdom, Thutmose III, c. 1450 BC, with later rebuilding
summary: Priests washed in this stone-lined pool, fed by groundwater, before touching anything holy; Amun's sacred geese lived beside it.
look: South of the main axis lies a rectangular pool, roughly 120 by 77 metres, lined with stone, with steps leading down into the water. At its north-west corner stand the giant scarab and the top of Hatshepsut's fallen obelisk; the tiered stands beside the lake are for the evening sound and light show.
story:
Every Egyptian temple of any size had a sacred lake, and Karnak's is one of the largest. Fed by groundwater, it rose and fell with the Nile, so its water was in a sense the flood itself, the primeval water from which the world began. The lake goes back to Thutmose III, though it was rebuilt and relined later.

Priests had to be pure. Herodotus, who travelled in Egypt in the 5th century BC, says Egyptian priests shaved their whole bodies every other day and bathed in cold water twice by day and twice by night. Water for the temple rituals was drawn from the lake, and on some festival nights small boats carrying images of the gods sailed on it.

The goose, like the ram, was sacred to Amun, and geese were kept by the lake. Around it archaeologists have found the houses of priests and storerooms for offerings.

Today it is the best place at Karnak to sit down for ten minutes, watch the light on the water, and let the temple sink in.
details: North-west corner: the giant granite scarab, and beside it the fallen tip of Hatshepsut's obelisk.
Look for the stone stairs leading down into the water on the sides of the lake.
Around the edges, look for the low ruins of priests' houses and storerooms.
When the wind drops, the pylons and columns are reflected in the water: the best quiet photo at Karnak.
fun_fact: Herodotus says Egyptian priests shaved every hair from their bodies every other day, so that no louse or other uncleanness could be on them while they served the gods.
narration:
In front of you is the Sacred Lake of Karnak, a stone-lined pool roughly 120 by 77 metres, filled not by a canal but by groundwater. It rose and fell with the Nile, so its water was, in a sense, the flood itself, the primeval water from which the Egyptians believed the world was born.

The lake goes back to Thutmose the Third, rebuilt over the centuries. Its job was purity. Before serving the god, priests washed here. Herodotus, the Greek historian who visited Egypt in the 5th century BC, was fascinated by Egyptian priests. He says they shaved their entire bodies every other day, so no louse could get near the god, and that they bathed in cold water twice every day and twice every night.

The lake was also a stage. On certain festival nights, small boats carrying images of the gods sailed on it. And the sacred geese of Amun, for the goose was one of his animals as well as the ram, were kept beside the water. Around the lake, excavators found the houses of priests and storerooms for offerings.

Today it is the best place in Karnak to sit down for a few minutes. The tiered seats are for the evening sound and light show.

Before you leave, look at the north-west corner of the lake. There is a giant stone beetle on a pedestal, and people are walking round it. That is your next stop.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC
summary: Amenhotep III's giant stone beetle is the rising sun in insect form. Walk round it, says a modern legend, and your wish comes true.
look: At the north-west corner of the Sacred Lake, a large granite scarab beetle sits on a tall stone pedestal carved with a dedication. Visitors walk round it in circles. The fallen tip of Hatshepsut's obelisk is a few steps away.
story:
The scarab is the dung beetle. Egyptians watched it roll a ball of dung across the ground and saw the sun being rolled across the sky from east to west. Young beetles emerge from the ball as if from nothing, so the beetle became the image of rebirth and self-creation. Its Egyptian name, kheper, also means 'to come into being', and the god Khepri was the sun at dawn, newly made each morning.

Amenhotep III dedicated this giant to Atum-Khepri, the sun in its evening and morning forms, and set it up in his vast mortuary temple on the West Bank, near the Colossi of Memnon. When that temple fell into ruin the scarab was brought across the river, perhaps in the time of Taharqa, whose building stood nearby.

Amenhotep loved scarabs. He issued large commemorative scarabs announcing events of his reign, all of them naming his queen, Tiye, and more than 200 survive.

The walking-round custom is modern. Guides will tell you three times for luck, seven for marriage, more for a baby; nobody knows who started it, and the numbers change with the guide.
details: Look at the beetle's broad head and folded legs: the sculptor knew his insect.
On the pedestal, find the hieroglyphic dedication of Amenhotep III.
Watch the circling visitors and count their laps: the numbers vary, and so do the promised rewards.
A few steps away: the fallen tip of Hatshepsut's obelisk.
fun_fact: One of Amenhotep III's commemorative scarabs boasts that he killed 102 lions with his own arrows in the first ten years of his reign.
narration:
This giant stone beetle is a scarab, carved for Amenhotep the Third about 3,400 years ago. And yes, people are walking round it. We will get to that.

The scarab is the dung beetle. Egyptians watched it roll a ball of dung across the ground and saw the sun being rolled across the sky. Even better, baby beetles crawl out of the ball as if made from nothing. So the beetle became the symbol of rebirth and daily renewal. Its Egyptian name, kheper, also means to come into being, and the god Khepri was the sun at dawn, newly made every morning.

Amenhotep dedicated this one to Atum Khepri, the sun in its evening and morning forms. It did not start here. It stood in his enormous mortuary temple on the West Bank, near the Colossi of Memnon, and was brought across the river later, perhaps in the time of Taharqa.

Amenhotep loved scarabs. He sent out large commemorative ones to announce his news. One brags that he killed 102 lions with his own arrows in his first ten years as king.

Now the custom. Guides will tell you: walk round three times for luck, seven for marriage, more for a baby. Nobody knows who started it, and the numbers change with the guide. It costs nothing, so go on. While you walk, look at the beetle's head and folded legs: the sculptor knew his insect.

period: New Kingdom, 20th Dynasty, c. 1180-1070 BC; gate of Ptolemy III, c. 240 BC
summary: The moon god's temple is Karnak's textbook, every part of a temple in order, and inside it a high priest dressed up as a king.
look: In the south-west corner of the precinct, walk through the pylon into a colonnaded court, then a small hall of columns, then the barque sanctuary and the rooms behind it, darker and lower as you go. South of the pylon rises the tall Ptolemaic gateway, Bab el-Amara, from which the Avenue of Sphinxes runs to Luxor Temple. Cleaned walls and ceilings inside show original paint.
story:
Khonsu was the son of Amun and Mut, the moon god; his name means 'the traveller', for the moon crossing the night sky. Ramesses III began this temple on the site of an older one, and later Ramesside kings carried on the decoration. Then the work passed to Herihor, High Priest of Amun under Ramesses XI. In the forecourt he appears in the role of a king, his name in a cartouche, offering like a pharaoh: an early sign that the priests of Amun were taking over the south.

Because it was built in one main campaign, it is the clearest example at Karnak of the standard plan: pylon, open court, hall of columns, sanctuary for the god's boat, and dark rooms behind, the floor rising and the light fading as you approach the god.

About 240 BC Ptolemy III, called Euergetes, 'the Benefactor' in Greek, built the great gateway in front, from which the Avenue of Sphinxes runs to Luxor Temple.

From 2006 to 2018 the American Research Center in Egypt cleaned and conserved the temple, bringing back painted ceilings and colour. Many blocks came from older monuments and carry reliefs set sideways or upside down.

A late legend, carved on the Bentresh stela now in the Louvre, tells how a statue of Khonsu travelled to a foreign land and drove a spirit out of a princess.
details: In the forecourt, find Herihor, the high priest, making offerings like a pharaoh, his name in a cartouche.
Look up at the cleaned ceilings in the hall and inner rooms, with their original paint.
Notice the floor rising and the light fading as you walk towards the sanctuary.
Look for reused blocks with reliefs set sideways or upside down.
Outside, to the south, Ptolemy III's Bab el-Amara gate: the avenue to Luxor Temple starts here.
fun_fact: In the Bentresh legend the grateful foreign prince kept Khonsu's statue for more than three years, until a dream persuaded him to send the god home.
narration:
This is the temple of Khonsu, the moon god, son of Amun and Mut. His name means the traveller, because the moon travels across the night sky.

Of all the buildings at Karnak, this is the one that best shows how a temple works, because it was built in one main campaign. Walk in and see: a gateway, an open court, a hall of columns, then the sanctuary for the god's sacred boat, and dark rooms behind it. As you go in, the floor rises and the light fades, until you reach the god.

Ramesses the Third began it around 1180 BC, and later kings carried on. Then the work passed to Herihor, High Priest of Amun. In the court he shows himself as if he were a king, with his name in a royal cartouche. It is one of the first signs that the priests of Amun were taking over the south.

The tall gateway outside was built about 240 BC by Ptolemy the Third, nicknamed Euergetes, the Benefactor in Greek. From there the Avenue of Sphinxes runs all the way to Luxor Temple.

Between 2006 and 2018, conservators of the American Research Center in Egypt cleaned the temple and found bright paint under the soot. A late legend says a statue of Khonsu once travelled abroad to cure a foreign princess, and her grateful father kept it for more than three years.

Before you leave, look up at the ceilings in the inner rooms, where the cleaned paint shines again.
